title: ‘Invasive species are doing their own work’: Indigenous ecological knowledge doesn't use a good-bad binary
dek: Species commonly labeled ‘invasive’—like European honeybees and Asian ladybugs—are viewed in indigenous ecological knowledge as fulfilling their own ecological roles, not as black-and-white enemies.
why: The densest information comes in the middle and latter sections, particularly worth hearing for the distinction between cultural fire and government-controlled burns, and the position of indigenous scientists in academia.
who: People working on ecological conservation, species diversity policy or cultural heritage, and those concerned about the position of indigenous scientists in academia.
skip: You can skip the opening pleasantries about the guest's appearance and bookshelf setup.

points.h: Honeybees don't come native or invasive—only working or not
points.body: The Oneida Nation's own orchards specifically borrow European honeybees from Florida farms for pollination; these bees are not native to North America, yet they're crucial labor for increasing yields. Cheyenne says indigenous languages often lack the word ‘invasive species’, instead using a framework where every species has work to do, and European honeybees are no exception. This directly contrasts with mainstream conservation discourse's default stance that ‘invasive = must eliminate’.

points.h: Endangered bumblebees are rebounding in indigenous-managed reserves
points.body: According to data from the Xerxes Society for Invertebrate Conservation, the rusty patched bumblebee has declined roughly 87% in recent decades and was listed as endangered in 2017; threats include introduced plant pests, lack of cultural burning, evergreen trees encroaching on meadow habitat, and pathogens from managed bees. But Cheyenne says this bee is making a strong comeback in the Oneida reserve, with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recently designating critical habitat nearby.

points.h: Cultural fire is not a government burn program with a different name
points.body: Both are controlled burns, but cultural fire is led by indigenous communities, with lower intensity, clearer intent, and timing determined by environmental cues like star positions; government and institutional burns are mostly about meeting area quotas. Indigenous community burns are motivated by ceremony or food sovereignty—a completely different logic from institutional burning's administrative goals.

points.h: Native American doctorate holders are less than one-third of one percent
points.body: According to 2024 article data, fewer than 2% of the U.S. population holds a doctorate; of that, only about one-third of one percent are Native Americans. Cheyenne says she rarely encountered scholars who looked like her or spoke like her growing up, which is why she once felt that getting a PhD ‘wasn't for someone like me’.

points.h: Dandelions tell the Tuscarora when their fish are spawning
points.body: Dandelions are a post-colonial introduction to North America, but their bloom period aligns with the spawning season of sturgeon culturally significant to the Tuscarora Nation and is still used as an important environmental signal. Similarly, Asian ladybugs were introduced for biological pest control and have crowded out native seven-spotted and nine-spotted ladybugs, yet they still eat aphids in the Three Sisters intercropping system and protect crops—so communities still acknowledge and respect the work they do.

points.h: The Haudenosaunee mosquito legend is about retaliation, not enmity
points.body: A Haudenosaunee story tells of two giant mosquitoes the size of trees that constantly attacked people paddling on the river; the people banded together to kill them, and when the giants fell, they scattered into countless tiny mosquitoes. Cheyenne says these small mosquitoes' existence today represents the mosquitoes retaliating for what the ancestors did—a ‘we struck first’ story, not one casting blood-sucking insects as pests to be eliminated.

points.h: The hardest part isn't fieldwork—it's defending why the work matters
points.body: Cheyenne says the most difficult part of her work isn't data analysis or writing, but constantly being asked ‘why is this important’ and ‘why should this shape policy’. She responds with one-on-one casual conversations, since a 12-minute academic presentation often can't convey the value of traditional ecological knowledge—the host notes with surprise that academia should be grateful for this knowledge rather than questioning it.
